A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same log-barrier approach to LP formulations of MDPs. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original DQN and DDPG benchmark experiments in Section 7 and a FrozenLake gradient-descent experiment in Appendix I.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds toy-MDP, robotics, sensitivity, baseline-comparison, and maximization-bias results in its appendices.

M1.justification: The main LP objective and DQN/DDPG algorithms are retained. Appendix R adds stochastic linear and tabular Q-learning adaptations using a maximized next-state target and a single Bellman-gap penalty, with explicit updates in Algorithms 3–4. These are limited procedural extensions of the existing barrier framework.

E1.justification: DQN coverage expands from three environments to five, adding MountainCar-v0 with shaped rewards and Pendulum-v1 with discretized actions. Appendix T.2 adds twelve robotics environments, while Appendices R and U introduce a four-state stochastic MDP and a maximization-bias scenario. Original benchmark coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Beyond the retained DQN/DDPG comparisons, v2 evaluates standard Q-learning, double Q-learning, and Lee and He's stochastic primal-dual Q-learning. Value iteration becomes a direct convergence comparator in Figure 6; in v1 it supplied the reference optimal Q-function. These substantially broaden the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce reward shaping, action discretization, 100,000-step toy-MDP training with linear or tabular representations, greedy versus reverse-greedy sampling, and controlled learning-rate and barrier-parameter sweeps. Figure 18 adds robotics evaluations extending to one million steps. The stated settings for the original DQN/DDPG benchmarks remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v1's FrozenLake barrier-coefficient study is retained and supplemented by learning-rate sweeps, off-policy sampling comparisons, enforcement-parameter ablations with underestimation/overestimation analyses, deep-RL barrier-coefficient sweeps, and a maximization-bias case study. These directly examine stability and mechanisms previously supported mainly by discussion.

E5.justification: Appendix T.2 newly specifies five random seeds per algorithm for robotics experiments. Table 4 supplies ± values without explicitly defining their statistic. Figures 1–2 retain the original ten-seed DQN and eight-seed DDPG mean/standard-deviation reporting; increased replication of those experiments is not established.

E6.justification: Substantial new results include faster value-iteration convergence in Figure 6, standard DQN outperforming the barrier variant on the added MountainCar and Pendulum tasks, and mixed robotics outcomes. Table 4 reports HandReach returns of -5.1 versus -3.2, but AdroitHandPen returns of -519.1 versus -635.9, for DDPG versus log-barrier DDPG. Figure 20 adds action-selection bias findings. These are newly reported comparisons, not demonstrated improvements over v1 under identical conditions.

T1.justification: Appendix H adds Theorem 5, deriving an explicit maximum-norm convergence bound and iteration requirement under an additional initialization bound. Appendix J adds Lemma 9 bounding the barrier minimizer's norm. These extend existing results; the central approximation-error, convexity, convergence, and policy-evaluation arguments are retained.

C1.justification: The central claims remain the log-barrier LP reformulation, approximation errors scaling linearly with the barrier parameter, gradient-descent convergence, and extensions to DQN/DDPG. The new introductory contribution summary and rewritten conclusion largely restate these claims rather than redefine the contribution.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly distinguishes tabular guarantees from nonlinear deep-RL behavior and substantially expands discussion of barrier sensitivity, feasibility failures, coupled parameter tuning, and speed–bias tradeoffs. Appendix R explains underestimation and overestimation under different enforcement strengths; Appendix T.2 explains identical robotics returns as shared manipulation failures.

D1.justification: v2 adds complete toy-MDP reward and transition matrices, the feature matrix, least-squares initialization, update pseudocode, and Table 3's training and barrier settings. Table 1 gains settings for the two added DQN tasks, and Appendices T–U document sweep ranges and bias-experiment parameters. This substantially expands reproducibility information.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including Applegate et al. (2021), Jaakkola et al. (1993), Munos and Szepesvari (2008), and Tsitsiklis (1994), supporting optimization and off-policy discussions. The introduction expands motivation concerning primal-dual methods, but the central positioning of barrier-based LP optimization remains unchanged.

P1.justification: The introduction gains motivation and a contribution summary, the conclusion is shortened and rewritten, and local explanations and title capitalization change. New appendices Q–U organize the added material, while the original section sequence and most existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 1 expands from three panels to five and is replotted. Figures 4–20 add convergence plots, sensitivity displays, value comparisons, robotics curves, and MDP diagrams; Tables 3–4 and Algorithms 3–4 are new. Existing figures, algorithms, and hyperparameter tables are also resized or relocated.

improvement.justification: v1 supported practical claims mainly through benchmark curves and one tabular sensitivity study. v2 substantially strengthens empirical scrutiny through targeted ablations, additional classical comparators, broader environments, and direct bias testing. Its explicit tuning limitations and reported failures make applicability clearer. Some supplementary protocols and uncertainty reporting remain incomplete, and favorable main-text summaries do not fully reflect the added negative results, but the gains in evidence and transparency are substantial.
